name: Anti-Caro: Fantasy Variation
pgn: e4 c6 d4 d5 f3 e6 Nc3 Bb4 Bf4
uci: e2e4 c7c6 d2d4 d7d5 f2f3 e7e6 b1c3 f8b4 c1f4
overview: We meet the Caro-Kann with the Fantasy Variation (3.f3) — Naroditsky's aggressive choice. White props up e4 and builds a big e4+d4 center, sidestepping the heavily-mapped Classical and Advance main lines and dragging Black into sharp, less-charted positions. Engine-sound for White (about +0.3) and a genuine out-of-prep weapon at club level.
keyIdeas: Support e4 with f3 and build the broad e4-d4 center
Pull Black off the well-known Caro main lines into fresh ground
If Black takes with ...dxe4, recapture and use the open f-file + center
Develop fast (Nc3, Be3, Qd2) and expand on the kingside

name: Anti-French: Advance Variation
pgn: e4 e6 d4 d5 e5 c5 c3 Nc6 Nf3 Bd7 Be2
uci: e2e4 e7e6 d2d4 d7d5 e4e5 c7c5 c2c3 b8c6 g1f3 c8d7 f1e2
overview: We meet the French with the Advance Variation (3.e5) — the most thematic, plan-based answer. White seizes space, locks the center, and plays for a kingside initiative while Black chips at the d4-base with ...c5. One fixed structure, clear plans, and it sidesteps the heavy Winawer theory — a reliable, low-memorization weapon (engine: comfortable edge).
keyIdeas: Gain space with e5 and fix the central structure
Defend the d4 chain-base with c3 and Nf3
Play on the kingside where your extra space tells
Meet ...c5 and ...Qb6 pressure with a3/Be2, keeping the chain intact

name: Anti-Pirc: Austrian Attack
pgn: e4 d6 d4 Nf6 Nc3 g6 f4 Bg7 Nf3
uci: e2e4 d7d6 d2d4 g8f6 b1c3 g7g6 f2f4 f8g7 g1f3
overview: We meet the Pirc with the Austrian Attack (4.f4) — the most aggressive try. White builds a broad e4+d4+f4 center and castles into a direct kingside attack against Black's fianchetto. Sharp, principled, and punishing if Black drifts (engine: clear White edge).
keyIdeas: Build the big e4-d4-f4 pawn center
Develop Nf3 and Be2/Bd3, castle short for the attack
Use f4-f5 to pry open Black's king
Stay alert to the freeing ...e5 and ...c5 breaks

name: Anti-Scandinavian: Main Line
pgn: e4 d5 exd5 Qxd5 Nc3 Qa5 d4 Nf6 Nf3 c6 Bc4 Bf5
uci: e2e4 d7d5 e4d5 d8d5 b1c3 d5a5 d2d4 g8f6 g1f3 c7c6 f1c4 c8f5
overview: We meet the Scandinavian by hitting the early queen: 2.exd5 Qxd5 3.Nc3 gains a tempo and a development lead. White follows with d4, Nf3 and easy, harmonious development while Black's queen has to find safety — a clean, low-risk edge (engine confirms).
keyIdeas: Hit the d5-queen with Nc3, gaining a tempo
Build the center with d4 and develop naturally
Convert the lead in development into an initiative
Target the squares Black's early ...Qxd5 left loose

name: Anti-Alekhine: Modern Variation
pgn: e4 Nf6 e5 Nd5 d4 d6 Nf3 Bg4 Be2
uci: e2e4 g8f6 e4e5 f6d5 d2d4 d7d6 g1f3 c8g4 f1e2
overview: We meet Alekhine's Defence with the Modern Variation (4.Nf3) — the soundest, most flexible setup. White declines the overextending Four Pawns and develops d4, Nf3, Be2, keeping a healthy space edge while Black's knight is chased to the rim. Solid and clearly better for White (engine confirms).
keyIdeas: Keep a sound space edge instead of overextending
Develop Nf3, Be2 and castle; meet ...Bg4 with h3
Use the e5-wedge to cramp Black
Expand with c4 when it gains time on the d5-knight

name: Anti-Modern: 150 Attack
pgn: e4 g6 d4 Bg7 Nc3 d6 Be3 a6 Qd2 b5
uci: e2e4 g7g6 d2d4 f8g7 b1c3 d7d6 c1e3 a7a6 d1d2 b7b5
overview: We meet the Modern Defence with the 150 Attack — a simple, crushing system. White plays Be3, Qd2 and f3, castles queenside, and storms the kingside with h4-h5 against Black's fianchetto. Easy to learn, hard to face, and objectively strong (engine: clear edge).
keyIdeas: Set up Be3 + Qd2 + f3 and castle queenside
Storm with h4-h5 to open Black's king
Trade the dark-squared bishops to weaken g7
Keep the center solid while you attack the wing

name: Anti-Sicilian: Rossolimo
pgn: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 g6 O-O
uci: e2e4 c7c5 g1f3 b8c6 f1b5 g7g6 e1g1
overview: We meet the Sicilian with the Rossolimo (3.Bb5) — the modern grandmaster anti-Sicilian. It sidesteps the vast Open Sicilian theory (Najdorf, Dragon, Sveshnikov) and goes for a clean structural game: damage Black's pawns with Bxc6 or keep the bishop pair, for a small but durable edge (engine confirms). Low theory, high practical value.
keyIdeas: Sidestep the Open Sicilian's enormous theory
Bxc6 to damage Black's structure, or retreat and keep the bishop pair
Play on the light squares and the d5 outpost
Aim for a small but lasting positional edge

name: Anti-Benoni/Benko: The d5 Push
pgn: d4 Nf6 c4 c5 d5 b5 cxb5 a6 bxa6 g6 Nc3 Bxa6 e4 Bxf1
uci: d2d4 g8f6 c2c4 c7c5 d4d5 b7b5 c4b5 a7a6 b5a6 g7g6 b1c3 c8a6 e2e4 a6f1
overview: We meet the Benoni/Benko with the principled d5 push — the line amateurs find hardest to face as White, now with a clear plan. White grabs the central and queenside space d5 grants, handles the Benko pawn sac on White's own terms, and keeps the extra space that makes these defenses hard for Black to justify (engine: solid White edge).
keyIdeas: Grab space with d5 and keep it
Meet ...b5 (Benko) by accepting/returning the pawn on your terms
Restrain Black's ...e6/...f5 and ...b5 breaks
Use the queenside space and the half-open lines

name: Anti-Englund Gambit
pgn: d4 e5 dxe5 Nc6 Nf3 Qe7 Nc3 Nxe5 e4 c6
uci: d2d4 e7e5 d4e5 b8c6 g1f3 d8e7 b1c3 c6e5 e2e4 c7c6
overview: We refute the Englund Gambit cleanly: 1.d4 e5 2.dxe5 — take the pawn and develop. With simple, accurate moves (Nf3, Nc3, e4) White keeps the extra pawn and reaches a near-winning position, while Black has nothing real for the material (engine: White clearly better, about +1.1).
keyIdeas: Take the e5-pawn and just develop
Meet ...Qe7/...Nc6 with Nf3 and Nc3, holding the pawn
Don't overreach; return the pawn only if it defuses tricks
Reach a sound, material-up middlegame
